content.thinking:
I'm treating this as a false alarm: the alert fired even though users saw nothing wrong and metrics stayed at baseline. The symptom is an error-rate alarm with no matching errors, and the write-up's "while <change>" clause has nothing to point to. The causal chain starts with that same mismatch, citing AL1 and T6.

I'm weighing whether to split the causal chain into two steps, with the second one stating that the rule fired without the service failing and that the record doesn't show why. I'll cite the alert rule's own series and the window reads. Deploys and feature flags weren't read, so I'll say in that step that no change was ruled out or confirmed.

I'm settling on the cause as the evidence stands: the alert rule fired even though no minute in the window read departed from baseline, and the record doesn't show why. Plain version: an error alarm went off while the service's measurements looked fine, and the reason it went off isn't recorded. I'm also noting that the same alarm could fire again without a real failure.

I'm thinking about whether the paging gap belongs under went_wrong: the alert rule isn't linked to an on-call incident, so nobody got paged by it. That's a fact about the setup rather than a cause of the false alarm, so I'll keep it separate and plan an action item to link the rule to on-call.

I'm weighing whether the contributing factors should include a check that the alert rule's condition gets verified against the service's metrics before it raises an alarm, since no such check shows up in what I've read. I'm also planning two action items: find out why HighErrorRate fired on io-shop when its own series showed no departure, and link that rule to an on-call paging route.

I'm settling on the action items now: first, looking into why the HighErrorRate rule on io-shop fired while its own series showed no departure from baseline, and second, deciding whether that rule should page on-call and linking it to a route if so. I'm leaving contributing factors empty, since the root cause is still unknown and nothing beyond it has been established. For went_well, Argus checked the alarm's claim against errors, latency, memory, and the rule's series, found none of it in the window, and marked the incident disproven.

I'm listing the three incident steps: the investigator reading back the per-minute metrics at the alert's time, Argus checking the alarm's claim against errors, latency, memory and the rule's own series and finding none of it there, and then marking the incident disproven. Nobody got paged, and I'm treating that as the one thing that went wrong rather than a cause. The limit I'm noting is that deploys, flags and logs weren't read, so the health of the service rests only on the metrics window.

I'm checking that the sentence about deploys and flags not being read is accounted for, since that limit is already noted in the step about assumptions.

action_items.item: Look into the HighErrorRate rule for io-shop and find out why it fired when its own series, as read, showed no departure from baseline.
Decide whether HighErrorRate on io-shop should page on-call. If it should, link the rule to an on-call paging route.

causal_chain.step: Nobody using io-shop was seen to have any problem. What was seen instead was the HighErrorRate alarm saying the error rate was above its threshold, while the metrics read showed no such errors.

The rule fired but the service did not fail: across errors, p50, p95, p99, memory and the alert rule's own series, no minute of the window read departed from baseline. The record does not show why the rule fired. Deploys and flags were not read, so no change was tied to the alarm and none was ruled out.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An error alarm for the shop service went off even though the service's own measurements showed nothing wrong, and the record does not show why the alarm went off.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read back the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on the alert's own time.
Argus checked the alarm's claim against errors, p50, p95, p99, memory and the alert rule's own series, and found it in none of them.
Argus closed the incident as DISPROVEN instead of leaving a false alarm open.

went_wrong: The alert was not linked to an on-call incident, so nobody was paged by it.

input.root_cause: The evidence does not show why the HighErrorRate rule fired: no minute of the window read, including the rule's own series, departed from the service's baseline. So the record shows no failure mechanism behind the alarm.
input.still_at_risk: The same alarm could fire again while the service is working normally.
input.symptom: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong; an error-rate alarm fired with no matching errors
